sentences.text: Magnapaulia was a herbivorous dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous in Baja California, northwestern Mexico.
The original researcher estimated that this creature reached lengths between 15 and 16.5 meters and could weigh as much as 8 metric tons.
A later study revised the length estimate to approximately 12.5 meters, noting it was the largest known lambeosaurine based on a specimen with an 80.3 cm humerus.
Subsequent calculations suggest the animal might have weighed up to 9.77 metric tons.
Distinctive anatomical features included tail chevrons that were four times longer than the vertebrae and front joint processes at the tail base forming a deep trough.
A tall crest of spines extended from the middle of the back to the middle of the tail, with each spine standing four times higher than the vertebrae.
Preserved skin impressions reveal large scales up to four centimeters wide surrounded by smaller hexagonal and rounded scales.
The species was first described in 1981 by William J. Morris as Lambeosaurus laticaudus based on a partial skeleton and skull.
The specific name laticaudus translates to broad tail in Latin.
The genus was elevated to a separate genus in 2012 by Prieto-Márquez, Chiappe, and Joshi.
The genus name honors Paul G. Haaga Jr., combining the Latin word for large with his first name.
Magnapaulia fossils were found in Upper Cretaceous rocks in Baja California, northwestern Mexico.
William J. Morris originally described the animal in 1981 as a possible species of Lambeosaurus named ?L. laticaudus.
Alberto Prieto-Márquez and colleagues assigned the animal to its own genus in 2012.
Morris used a question mark for the species name because a complete crest had not been found at the time.
Morris considered the species semiaquatic, interpreting its large size and high, narrow tail as adaptations for swimming.
Morris thought a healed broken femur was evidence that a terrestrial animal would not have survived long enough to heal such an injury.
Magnapaulia is classified within the subfamily Lambeosaurinae.
Cladistic analysis places Magnapaulia closest to Velafrons, forming a southern clade sister to northern Asian and North American lambeosaurines.
Magnapaulia was assigned to the subfamily Lambeosaurinae in 2012.
A 2012 cladistic analysis placed Magnapaulia close to Velafrons, identifying it as the sister species.
The parent group of Magnapaulia is Lambeosaurini.
Magnapaulia belongs to the family Hadrosauridae.
Magnapaulia is classified in the class Ornithischia.
Fossils date to the late Campanian stage, approximately 73.6 to 73 million years ago.
Magnapaulia laticaudus is the only known species of this extinct lambeosaurine ornithopod dinosaur.
The 2012 study dated the fossils to the late Campanian stage, approximately 73.6 to 73 million years ago.
The time range for Magnapaulia is the Campanian stage, from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
Between 1981 and 2012, researchers debated whether the remains belonged to Lambeosaurus, Hypacrosaurus, or represented a valid new genus.
